chains.earliest_control: phishing-resistant MFA required for the highly privileged roles (in the tenant)
chains.name: Organization takeover through an owner's Microsoft 365 account

steps.text: An adversary-in-the-middle phishing page relays an owner's Microsoft 365 sign-in: the tenant does not enforce phishing-resistant MFA (MS.AAD.3.1v1), not even for the highly privileged roles both owners hold (H1).

The same identity holds GitHub ownership. The owner who reports a TOTP app has no phishing-resistant method on record (GH-ID-02; A5), and a TOTP code can be relayed by the same kit; password reset mail for the account lands in the already-captured tenant mailbox (H1).

As owner, the adversary authorizes an approved-looking OAuth app or creates a fine-grained token: OAuth app access restrictions are off and fine-grained tokens need no approval (GH-TOK-01, GH-TOK-03; C1, C2), so the grant survives a password reset.

chains.earliest_control: default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions set to read-only
chains.name: Malicious workflow through a public repository

steps.text: Anyone can fork field-notes and open a pull request; its pull_request_target workflow checks out and builds the pull request's head, and runs regardless of approval settings (D3; GH-ACT-03).
The workflow runs in the base repository's context with a GITHUB_TOKEN that defaults to read and write (GH-ACT-02; D1).
The deployment credential among the organization secrets is available to all repositories, field-notes included (GH-ACT-06; D2), so the build script can read it and send it out.

chains.earliest_control: outside collaborators' access reviewed at least quarterly, with only owners inviting
chains.name: Persistence through a dormant collaborator and a stale webhook

steps.text: The former vendor's staff member keeps write access to client-portal with no two-factor authentication (B3; GH-ID-01), so that one password opens a client repository.
No collaborator review is on record (GH-MEM-03), so the access was never removed when the engagement ended.

Separately, the ci-old webhook still sends organization event payloads to a decommissioned server's name, which has answered with success since October 2026 (F1, F2); whoever operates it now receives them (F3; GH-WH-03).
